# Shock

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Cardiology and angiology > Syncope and shock > Shock*

[Original Article Link](/library/kO0msT)

---

## Summary

Shock is a life-threatening circulatory disorder that leads to tissue <u>hypoxia</u> and a disturbance in <u>microcirculation</u>. The numerous causes of shock are classified into <u>hypovolemic shock</u> (e.g., following massive blood/fluid loss), <u>cardiogenic shock</u> (e.g., as a result of <u>acute heart failure</u>), <u>obstructive shock</u> (e.g., due to <u>cardiac tamponade</u>), and <u>distributive shock</u> (due to redistribution of body fluids), which is further classified into <u>septic</u>, <u>anaphylactic</u>, and <u>neurogenic shock</u>. Common clinical findings are <u>hypotension</u> and abnormal <u>heart rate</u> (most commonly <u>tachycardia</u>; <u>bradycardia</u> in <u>neurogenic shock</u>) accompanied by specific symptoms related to the cause of shock. Diagnosis is mostly clinical but measurement of functional parameters (e.g., <u>PCWP</u>, <u>cardiac output</u>, <u>SVR</u>) can help distinguish between the different <u>types of shock</u>. <u>Management of shock</u> involves circulatory support and treatment of the underlying cause. Shock is associated with a very high <u>mortality rate</u>.

---

## Overview

### Definitions




* Shock (circulatory shock): a life-threatening disorder of the <u>circulatory system</u> that results in inadequate organ <u>perfusion</u> and tissue <u>hypoxia</u>, leading to metabolic disturbances and, ultimately, irreversible organ damage [[1]](/library/xgYExo)[[2]](/library/nhY7eK)

* Shock index = <u>pulse</u> rate/systolic blood pressure 

* Normal range: 0.4–0.7

* > 1 (positive <u>shock index</u>): consistent with circulatory shock





### <u>Types of shock</u>




| <br>Overview of the types of shock [[3]](/library/Tob6Yu)[[4]](/library/_SX5XB)[[5]](/library/BNXzWA)<br> |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Type |  | Etiology of shock |  | <br>Typical <u>hemodynamic parameters</u> [[6]](/library/SlXywy)<br> | Distinguishing clinical features | Treatment options |
| <br><u>Hypovolemic shock</u>  (includes <u>hemorrhagic shock</u>) |  | <br><br>* Fluid loss (from <u>GI tract</u>, <u>skin</u>, <u>kidneys</u>, or <u>third spacing</u>)<br><br>* Hemorrhage<br><br><br> |  | <br><br>* ↓ <u>CVP</u><br><br>* ↓↓ <u>PCWP</u><br><br>* ↓ CO<br><br>* ↑ <u>SVR</u><br><br>* ↑ HR<br><br>* ↓ SVO<sub>2</sub><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Cold, clammy extremities, slow <u>capillary refill</u><br><br>* Nondistended jugular <u>veins</u> (sometimes referred to as “empty <u>heart</u>”)<br><br>* Decreased <u>skin turgor</u>, dry <u>mucous membranes</u><br><br>* Features of underlying etiology: e.g., <u>signs of GI bleeding</u>, <u>diarrhea</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Fluid resuscitation</u><br><br>* <u>Blood transfusion</u><br><br>* <u>Hemostatic control</u><br><br><br> |
| <u>Cardiogenic shock</u> |  | <br><br>* Cardiac <u>ischemia</u><br><br>* <u>Arrhythmias</u><br><br>* Valvulopathy<br><br>* Cardiotoxic substance exposure<br><br><br> |  | <br><br>* ↑ <u>CVP</u><br><br>* ↑ <u>PCWP</u><br><br>* ↓↓ CO<br><br>* ↑ <u>SVR</u><br><br>* Variable HR<br><br>* ↓ SVO<sub>2</sub><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Cold, clammy extremities, poor <u>capillary refill</u><br><br>* Elevated <u>JVP</u> and distended neck <u>veins</u> (sometimes referred to as “full <u>heart</u>”)<br><br>* <u>Clinical features of heart failure</u><br><br>* Features of underlying etiology: e.g., <u>chest pain</u>, <u>palpitations</u>, <u>syncope</u>, new/worsening <u>murmur</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Administration of <u>IV fluids</u> according to <u>fluid responsiveness</u> (see also “<u>Fluid challenge</u>”)<br><br>* <u>Inotropic</u> support<br><br>* <u>Vasopressors</u><br><br>* <u>Diuretics</u><br><br>* <u>Treatment of refractory acute heart failure</u><br><br><br> |
| <u>Obstructive shock</u> |  | <br><br>* Impairment of <u>diastolic</u> filling of the <u>right ventricle</u> (e.g., <u>cardiac tamponade</u>)<br><br>* Obstruction of <u>venous return</u> (e.g., <u>tension pneumothorax</u>)<br><br>* ↑ Ventricular <u>afterload</u> (e.g., <u>massive pulmonary embolism</u>)<br><br><br> |  | <br><br>* ↑ <u>CVP</u><br><br>* ↑ or ↓ <u>PCWP</u><br><br>* ↓↓ CO<br><br>* ↑ <u>SVR</u><br><br>* ↑ HR<br><br>* ↓ SVO<sub>2</sub><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Cold, clammy extremities, poor <u>capillary refill</u><br><br>* Elevated <u>JVP</u> and distended neck <u>veins</u><br><br>* Features of underlying etiology: e.g., <u>chest pain</u>, diminished breath sounds, <u>tracheal deviation</u>, muffled <u>heart</u> tones, <u>clinical features of DVT</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Fluid resuscitation</u><br><br>* Interventions to relieve obstruction, e.g.:<br><br>* <u>Pericardiocentesis</u><br><br>* <u>Needle thoracostomy</u> followed by <u>tube thoracostomy</u><br><br>* <u>Thrombolysis</u><br><br><br> |
| <u>Distributive shock</u> | <br><u>Septic shock</u> (most common)<br> | <br><br>* Infection<br><br>* <u>Bacteremia</u><br><br>* See “Etiology” in “<u>Sepsis</u>” for details.<br><br><br> |  | <br><br>* ↓ <u>CVP</u><br><br>* Normal or ↓ <u>PCWP</u><br><br>* ↑ or ↓ CO<br><br>* ↓↓ <u>SVR</u><br><br>* ↑ HR<br><br>* ↑ SVO<sub>2</sub><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Early: flushed, warm <u>skin</u>, normal <u>capillary refill</u><br><br>* Late: cold, pale <u>skin</u> with delayed <u>capillary refill</u><br><br>* <u>Features of sepsis</u>: e.g., <u>fever</u>, <u>SIRS criteria</u><br><br>* Features of underlying infection: e.g., signs of <u>typical pneumonia</u>, <u>meningismus</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Fluid resuscitation</u><br><br>* <u>Vasopressors</u><br><br>* <u>Antibiotics</u><br><br>* Infectious source control (e.g., <u>abscess</u> drainage, <u>surgery</u>)<br><br><br> |
| <u>Anaphylactic shock</u> | <br><br>* Exposure to <u>allergens</u> (e.g., food, <u>bee stings</u>, drug reactions)<br><br>* See “Etiology” in “<u>Anaphylaxis</u>” for details.<br><br><br> |  | <br><br>* ↓ <u>CVP</u><br><br>* ↓↓ <u>PCWP</u><br><br>* ↑ or ↓ CO<br><br>* ↓↓ <u>SVR</u><br><br>* ↑ HR<br><br>* ↑ SVO<sub>2</sub><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Suspected or confirmed <u>allergen</u> exposure<br><br>* Rapid onset (minutes to hours)<br><br>* <u>Clinical features of anaphylaxis</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Epinephrine</u><br><br>* <u>Fluid resuscitation</u><br><br><br> |  |
| <br><u>Neurogenic shock</u><br> | <br>* <u>CNS</u> injury (e.g., <u>spinal cord injury</u> <u>ICH</u>, <u>TBI</u>)<br><br> |  | <br><br>* ↓ <u>CVP</u><br><br>* ↓↓ <u>PCWP</u><br><br>* ↓ CO<br><br>* ↓↓ <u>SVR</u><br><br>* ↓ HR<br><br>* Normal or ↑ SVO<sub>2</sub><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Flushed, warm <u>skin</u><br><br>* <u>Bradycardia</u><br><br>* Features of underlying etiology: neurological deficits (e.g., <u>flaccid paralysis</u> in spinal trauma)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Fluid resuscitation</u><br><br>* <u>Vasopressors</u><br><br>* <u>Atropine</u> for <u>bradycardia</u><br><br><br> |  |
| <br>Key <u>CVP</u>: right <u>heart</u> <u>preload</u> <u>PCWP</u>: <u>pulmonary capillary wedge pressure</u> (a <u>surrogate</u> marker for <u>preload</u>)  CO: <u>cardiac output</u> (CO = HR × <u>stroke volume</u>)  <u>SVR</u>: <u>systemic vascular resistance</u> (a <u>surrogate</u> marker for <u>afterload</u>) HR: <u>heart rate</u> SVO<sub>2</sub>: mixed venous content |  |  |  |  |  |  |

### Hemodynamic parameters in shock




| <br><u>Typical hemodynamic parameters of types of shock</u> [[3]](/library/Tob6Yu)[[4]](/library/_SX5XB)[[5]](/library/BNXzWA)[[6]](/library/SlXywy)<br> |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Type | Estimated <u>cardiac output</u> (CO) | Estimated <u>preload</u> (e.g., <u>PCWP</u>) | Estimated <u>afterload</u> (e.g., <u>SVR</u>) | <br>Likelihood of <u>fluid responsiveness</u> <br> |
| <u>Hypovolemic</u> | <br>* ↓<br><br> | <br>* ↓<br><br> | <br>* ↑<br><br> | <br>* ↑<br><br> |
| Cardiogenic | <br>* ↓↓<br><br> | <br>* ↑<br><br> | <br>* ↑<br><br> | <br>* ↓<br><br> |
| Obstructive | <br>* ↓↓<br><br> | <br>* ↓ Or ↑<br><br> | <br>* ↑<br><br> | <br>* ↑<br><br> |
| Distributive | <br><br>* Neurogenic: ↓<br><br>* <u>Septic</u> and <u>anaphylactic</u><br><br>* Early: ↑<br><br>* Late: ↓<br><br><br> | <br>* Usually ↓<br><br> | <br>* ↓↓<br><br> | <br>* ↑<br><br> |





### <u>Stages of shock</u>




The following stages may not occur in cases of sudden severe cardiovascular collapse , and the progression between stages in <u>septic shock</u> can be indistinct.




| Stages of shock |  |
| --- | --- |
| Stage | Characteristics |
| 1. Preshock | <br><br>* Peripheral <u>vasoconstriction</u> <br><br>* Manifests with cold, clammy extremities and increased <u>capillary refill time</u><br><br>* Decreased <u>capillary</u> <u>hydrostatic pressure</u> → increased absorption of <u>interstitial</u> fluids into <u>intravascular space</u> to help maintain blood pressure<br><br>* Peripheral <u>vasoconstriction</u> may be absent in <u>distributive shock</u>.<br><br>* <u>Tachycardia</u> (Patients with <u>neurogenic shock</u> may present with <u>bradycardia</u>.)<br><br>* <u>Oliguria</u><br><br><br> |
| <br>2. Shock  (progressive phase) | <br><br>* Worsening <u>hypotension</u><br><br>* <u>Hypoperfusion</u> of peripheral tissues → generalized tissue <u>hypoxia</u> → <u>anaerobic metabolism</u> in the underperfused organs → <u>lactic acidosis</u> , which in turn causes:<br><br>* Worsening <u>tachypnea</u><br><br>* Precapillary dilation and postcapillary constriction of the blood vessels → pooling and stasis of blood in the <u>capillary</u> bed → decreased <u>cardiac output</u> and formation of microthrombi in the <u>capillaries</u> → <u>DIC</u> and further <u>hypoxic</u> injury to tissues<br><br>* <u>Acidosis</u>, cerebral <u>hypoperfusion</u> → <u>altered mental status</u><br><br><br> |
| <br>3. End-organ dysfunction (stage of decompensation) | <br><br>* Cerebral <u>hypoxia</u> → <u>autonomic dysfunction</u><br><br>* <u>Myocardial</u> <u>ischemia</u> → decreased <u>cardiac output</u><br><br>* Widespread cell <u>necrosis</u> causes:<br><br>* Release of <u>lysosomal</u> enzymes → further tissue injury → worsening of shock<br><br>* Activation of the <u>immune system</u> → release of <u>cytokines</u> → <u>DIC</u>, further tissue damage<br><br>* <u>Bowel ischemia</u> → <u>bacteremic</u> <u>sepsis</u><br><br>* Can create a vicious cycle, leading to irreversible <u>multiple organ failure</u><br><br><br> |

---

## Diagnostics

Routine investigations can help identify the shock subtype but are not required for diagnosis. Consider further investigations if the subtype remains uncertain.




> [!TIP]
> Shock is a clinical diagnosis.




### Routine investigations




Findings allow for evaluation of the following:




* <u>Global</u> <u>hypoperfusion</u>

* ↑ <u>Lactate</u> (> 2 mmol/L) suggests tissue <u>hypoperfusion</u> and is associated with poorer outcomes  [[11]](/library/UMbbL8)[[12]](/library/1Ba2-5)

* <u>ABG</u>

* <u>Metabolic acidosis</u>: ↑ <u>base excess</u>, ↓ <u>HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup></u>

* <u>Contraction alkalosis</u>: ↑ <u>HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup></u>

* Underlying etiology

* <u>CBC</u>

* ↓ <u>Hb</u>, ↓ <u>Hct</u>: suggests hemorrhage

* <u>Leukopenia</u> or <u>leukocytosis</u>: suggests <u>sepsis</u>

* <u>BMP</u>: ↑ <u>BUN/Cr ratio</u>, <u>hyponatremia</u>, and other <u>laboratory findings of hypovolemia</u>

* <u>Septic workup</u>: e.g., <u>urinalysis</u>, <u>blood cultures</u>

* <u>ECG</u>: Findings can show evidence of cardiogenic etiology, e.g., <u>arrhythmias</u> , <u>acute coronary syndrome</u> , signs of <u>cardiomyopathy</u>.

* <u>CXR</u>

* <u>Pneumonia</u> : suggests <u>sepsis</u>

* <u>Pulmonary edema</u> , <u>cardiac enlargement</u>, or <u>pleural effusions</u> : suggests cardiogenic etiology

* <u>Pneumothorax</u> : suggests obstructive etiology

* Complications or <u>end-organ dysfunction</u>

* <u>Hypoglycemia</u> or <u>hyperglycemia</u>

* <u>Electrolyte</u> abnormalities

* <u>Renal function tests</u>: ↑ <u>BUN</u>, ↑ <u>creatinine</u>, other <u>signs of AKI</u> or <u>ATN</u> (e.g., on <u>urinalysis</u>)

* <u>Liver chemistries</u>: elevated in <u>shock liver</u>

* <u>Coagulation panel</u>: suggestive of <u>DIC</u>, <u>acute traumatic coagulopathy</u>, or <u>acute liver failure</u>





> [!TIP]
> In all patients with shock, immediately measure <u>ABGs</u>, <u>lactate</u> levels, <u>capillary</u> <u>glucose</u>, perform an <u>ECG</u>, and order a <u>chest x-ray</u> and general <u>laboratory studies</u>.




> [!TIP]
> Compare any available previous studies to the patient's current test results. Previous studies can help determine if alterations to any laboratory or imaging studies are new and likely the cause of shock, or if they are caused by chronic conditions (e.g., <u>CKD</u>, chronic <u>heart failure</u>).

### Further investigations




Further studies should be guided by clinical suspicion of the underlying cause.




| Further diagnostic studies for patients in shock |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| <u>Type of shock</u> |  | Studies to consider |
| Unclear after initial evaluation |  | <br>* <u>Rapid assessment by cardiac echo</u>  [[4]](/library/_SX5XB)[[13]](/library/ACbRuD)<br><br> |
| <u>Hypovolemic shock</u> | <br><u>Hemorrhagic shock</u> <br> | <br><br>* Repeat <u>CBC</u>: ↓ <u>Hb</u> and <u>Hct</u> (can be normal initially)<br><br>* <u>Type and screen</u> <u>blood products</u>.<br><br>* To identify hemorrhage source<br><br>* <u>FAST scan</u>: to identify intraabdominal hemorrhage<br><br>* <u>X-ray</u>: to identify <u>pelvic</u> ring <u>fractures</u>, <u>hemothorax</u><br><br>* <u>DRE</u>: to identify active <u>GI bleeding</u><br><br><br> |
| Nonhemorrhagic shock | <br><br>* <u>Insensible fluid losses</u>: <u>fever workup</u> (see also “Diagnostics” in “<u>Heatstroke</u>”)<br><br>* <u>Third space fluid loss</u>: CT abdomen to evaluate for <u>pancreatitis</u> or <u>bowel obstruction</u><br><br>* GI losses: See “Diagnostics” in “<u>Nausea and vomiting</u>” and “<u>Diarrhea</u>.”<br><br>* Renal losses: urine <u>electrolytes</u>, urine <u>creatinine</u><br><br><br> |  |
| <u>Cardiogenic shock</u> |  | <br><br>* <u>BNP</u> and <u>NT-proBNP</u> compared to baseline<br><br>* <u>ECG</u>: <u>myocardial infarction</u>, <u>cardiac arrhythmias</u>, signs of ventricular <u>hypertrophy</u><br><br>* Cardiac markers: ↑ <u>troponin I</u> and <u>troponin T</u> in <u>acute coronary syndrome</u><br><br>* <u>Echocardiography</u>: to identify valvular lesions, ventricular dysfunction, <u>pericardial effusion</u><br><br><br> |
| <u>Obstructive shock</u> |  | <br><br>* <u>Echocardiography</u> and <u>POCUS</u>: findings depend on the etiology<br><br>* <u>X-ray</u> or CT chest: can identify <u>pneumothorax</u><br><br>* <u>CT pulmonary angiography</u> or <u>V/Q scan</u>: for suspected <u>pulmonary embolism</u>, <u>aortic dissection</u><br><br><br> |
| <u>Distributive shock</u> | <u>Septic shock</u> | <br><br>* Cultures: e.g., blood and urine<br><br>* <u>Acute phase reactants</u>: e.g., <u>ESR</u>, <u>CRP</u>, <u>procalcitonin</u><br><br>* See also “<u>Septic workup</u>.”<br><br><br> |
| <u>Anaphylactic shock</u> | <br><br>* Diagnosis is mostly clinical.<br><br>* Serum <u>mast-cell tryptase</u> if diagnosis is uncertain<br><br>* See also “<u>Diagnostic criteria for anaphylaxis</u>.”<br><br><br> |  |
| <u>Neurogenic shock</u> | <br>* Imaging studies can help identify the underlying injury (e.g., CT or <u>MRI</u> <u>spine</u>, CT or <u>MRI</u> <u>brain</u>).<br><br> |  |





> [!TIP]
> If <u>hemorrhagic shock</u> is suspected, perform blood <u>type and screen</u> and <u>crossmatch</u> as soon as possible. <u>Emergency issue blood products</u>, e.g., <u>Blood type O</u> <u>Rh-negative</u> blood, can be given immediately; however, type-specific and <u>crossmatched</u> <u>blood products</u> are preferred as soon as they become available.

## Monitoring

Monitoring parameters can be used as treatment targets and should be tailored to the patient.




| <br><u>Monitoring parameters for patients with shock</u> [[7]](/library/kmbmf8)[[24]](/library/WPXPdy)<br> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Variable |  | Parameters |
| <u>Clinical features in shock</u> | <u>Vital signs</u> | <br><br>* <u>Heart rate</u>: Aim for resolution of compensatory <u>tachycardia</u> and correction of <u>arrhythmias</u>.<br><br>* Blood pressure: For most patients, target an <u>MAP</u> of ≥ 65 mm Hg.<br><br><br> |
| Others | <br><br>* <u>Volume status assessment</u><br><br>* Resolution of <u>signs of end-organ hypoperfusion</u>, including:<br><br>* Normal mental status<br><br>* Normal <u>capillary refill</u><br><br>* Improvements in <u>skin</u> color and temperature<br><br>* Urine output (for most patients): target > 0.5 mL/kg/hour<br><br><br> |  |
| Laboratory | <u>Lactate</u> | <br><br>* Aim for a <u>lactate</u> level â¤ 2 mEq/L.<br><br>* Monitor for changes over time (i.e., <u>lactate</u> clearance).  [[25]](/library/bfcHkb0)<br><br><br> |
| <br><u>Base deficit</u> (BD) | <br><br>* Measure of <u>metabolic acidosis</u><br><br>* Can aid the <u>classification of hemorrhagic shock</u>  [[26]](/library/7zX4800)[[27]](/library/HzXK800)<br><br>* BD ≤ 2: frequently seen in patients with no shock<br><br>* BD ≥10: frequently seen in patients with severe shock<br><br><br> |  |
| <br><u>SvO<sub>2</sub></u> and <u>ScvO<sub>2</sub></u> [[6]](/library/SlXywy)[[28]](/library/3lXS9y)[[29]](/library/RlXl9y)<br> | <br><br>* Require access to central venous blood<br><br>* Used as markers of <u>oxygen delivery</u> and consumption in the tissues [[29]](/library/RlXl9y)<br><br>* Clinical applications<br><br>* Estimating <u>cardiac output</u> in conjunction with other diagnostic tests<br><br>* Used as a target in <u>septic shock</u><br><br>* Can be serially measured and interpreted along with other parameters of cardiopulmonary function  [[30]](/library/hlXc9y)<br><br>* <u>SvO<sub>2</sub></u> > 90%: marker of <u>microcirculatory</u> shunt ; confers a worse prognosis [[6]](/library/SlXywy)<br><br>* <u>SvO<sub>2</sub></u> < 65% (<u>ScvO<sub>2</sub></u> < 70%): possibly ↓ CO or <u>anemia</u><br><br>* <u>SvO<sub>2</sub></u> ≥ 65% (<u>ScvO<sub>2</sub></u> ≥ 70%) with:<br><br>* <u>Lactate</u> â¤ 2 mEq/L: can be considered normal<br><br>* <u>Lactate</u> > 2 mEq/L: possibly tissue <u>hypoxia</u> resulting from <u>sepsis</u>, or <u>microcirculatory</u> alterations<br><br><br> |  |
| Device-based | <br><br><u>Central venous pressure</u>(<u>CVP</u>) [[6]](/library/SlXywy)[[31]](/library/CkXqJy)<br> | <br><br>* Marker of <u>right atrial pressure</u> and, indirectly, <u>venous return</u>, ventricular <u>preload</u>, and <u>volume status</u><br><br>* Commonly used target for patients in shock: 8–12 mm Hg   [[6]](/library/SlXywy)<br><br>* < 8 mm Hg: suggests <u>hypovolemia</u><br><br>* > 12 mm Hg: suggests <u>volume overload</u><br><br>* <u>CVP</u> is also affected by thoracic, <u>pericardial</u>, and abdominal pressures.<br><br><br> |
| <br>Cardiac function [[6]](/library/SlXywy)<br> | <br><br>* Normal <u>cardiac output</u>: 4–8 L/minute<br><br>* <u>Cardiac index</u>: > 2.2 L/min/m<sup>2</sup><br><br><br> |  |
| Bedside <u>echocardiography</u>/<u>POCUS</u> | <br><br>* <u>Rapid assessment by cardiac echo</u> (RACE)<br><br>* <u>IVC</u> diameter and <u>IVC</u> collapsibility<br><br><br> |  |





> [!WARNING]
> Signs of an inadequate response to <u>fluid resuscitation</u> include persistently ↑ <u>heart rate</u>, ↓ blood pressure, ↓ <u>CVP</u>, and ↓ urine output (< 0.5 mL/kg/hour).




> [!WARNING]
> <u>Oxygen saturation</u> from peripheral <u>venous blood gases</u> should not be misinterpreted as <u>SvO<sub>2</sub></u> or <u>ScvO<sub>2</sub></u>.




* Invasive hemodynamic monitoring: typically reserved for patients with severe shock

* Most patients: urinary catheter to assess urine output

* Patients requiring <u>vasopressors</u> [[7]](/library/kmbmf8)

* <u>Central venous line</u>: can be used for <u>CVP</u> monitoring and ScVO<sub>2</sub> sampling

* <u>Arterial line</u>: can be used for <u>invasive blood pressure monitoring</u> and frequent <u>ABG sampling</u>

* Select patients with <u>refractory shock</u>, RV dysfunction, or high risk of <u>pulmonary edema</u> with uncertain fluid status: <u>pulmonary artery catheterization</u>  [[7]](/library/kmbmf8)[[32]](/library/0PXeWy)

* Protocolized resuscitation targets: e.g., consider <u>lactate-guided fluid resuscitation strategy</u> or <u>early goal-directed therapy</u> (<u>EGDT</u>) in <u>sepsis</u>.

---

## Hypovolemic shock

### Etiology




* Hemorrhage

* <u>Postpartum hemorrhage</u>

* <u>Upper GI bleeding</u> (e.g., <u>variceal bleeding</u>, <u>PUD</u>)

* Blunt/penetrating trauma

* Ruptured <u>aneurysm</u> or <u>hematoma</u>

* <u>Arteriovenous fistula</u>

* Nonhemorrhagic fluid loss 

* GI loss (e.g., <u>diarrhea</u>, <u>vomiting</u>)

* Increased <u>insensible fluid loss</u> (e.g., <u>burns</u>)

* <u>Third space fluid loss</u> (e.g., <u>bowel obstruction</u>, <u>pancreatitis</u>)

* Renal fluid loss (e.g., <u>adrenal insufficiency</u>, drug-induced diuresis)





### Pathophysiology




Loss of <u>intravascular</u> fluid volume → ↓ <u>preload</u> and <u>SV</u> → ↓ CO → compensatory ↑ <u>SVR</u> and HR




### Management [[4]](/library/_SX5XB)[[7]](/library/kmbmf8)[[8]](/library/LiXwHB)




The priority of <u>immediate hemodynamic support</u> is aggressive <u>fluid resuscitation</u> to achieve <u>euvolemia</u>. Further treatment depends on the etiologic category of <u>hypovolemia</u> (hemorrhagic vs. nonhemorrhagic).




#### Hemorrhagic shock




* <u>Blood products</u>: Transfuse as soon as possible.

* Ensure adequate <u>vascular access</u> and equipment (e.g., tubing) for <u>blood products</u>.

* Consider <u>emergency transfusion</u> of uncrossmatched <u>blood type O</u> <u>rhesus negative</u> units.

* Switch to <u>crossmatched</u> <u>blood transfusions</u> as soon as available.

* If <u>massive transfusion</u> is expected : Consider transfusing <u>packed RBC</u>, <u>FFP</u>, and <u>platelet</u> concentrate in a 1:1:1 <u>ratio</u>.  [[51]](/library/SIbyXE)

* Consider the use of specialized infusers that allow for rapid administration of warmed blood.

* <u>Hemostatic control</u>: should be prioritized

* Begin immediate bedside measures: e.g., applying pressure, <u>suturing</u>, or stapling <u>open wounds</u>.

* Consult specialist based on underlying etiology and risk <u>stratification</u>: e.g., <u>surgery</u>, gastroenterology, <u>OB-GYN</u>, interventional radiology.

* Ensure definitive care: See “<u>Management of trauma patients</u>,” ”<u>Treatment of GI bleeding</u>,” “<u>Abnormal uterine bleeding</u>,” “<u>Antepartum hemorrhage</u>,” and “<u>Postpartum hemorrhage</u>.”

* Additional steps to consider [[52]](/library/M1VMht0)[[53]](/library/2PVTVu0)[[54]](/library/fPVkVu0)

* <u>Tranexamic acid</u> for severe traumatic injury within 3 hours of injury DOSAGE [[55]](/library/_jX51y)[[56]](/library/zjXr1y)

* <u>Classification of hemorrhagic shock</u> to help prioritize definitive care and monitor response to treatment





| Classification of hemorrhagic shock |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Class | I | II | III | IV |
| <br>Blood loss (% of total blood volume) | < 15% | 15–30% | 30–40% | > 40% |
| <br>Volume loss (in an average adult) | ∼ 750 mL | ∼ 750–1500 mL | ∼ 1500–2000 mL | > 2000 mL |
| <br><u>Heart rate</u> (bpm)<br> | 70–99 | 100–120 | 120–140 | > 140 |
| Systolic blood pressure | Normal | Normal | ↓ | ↓ |
| <u>Pulse pressure</u> | Normal or ↑<br> | ↓ | ↓ | ↓ |
| <br><u>Respiratory rate</u> (rpm)<br> | Normal | 20–30 | 30–40 | > 35 |
| Urine output | > 30 mL/hour | 20–30 mL/hour | 5–15 mL/hour | Absent |
| Mental status | Normal | Mildly anxious | Anxious, confused | Confused, <u>lethargic</u><br> |





> [!TIP]
> Upon suspecting <u>hemorrhagic shock</u>, perform blood grouping and <u>cross-matching</u> and have <u>packed RBCs</u> at hand for <u>transfusion</u>.




> [!WARNING]
> Uncrossmatched <u>RBC</u> type O negative units can be transfused if the hemorrhage is severe.




#### Nonhemorrhagic hypovolemic shock




* Treatment of the underlying etiology to stop fluid losses, including:

* GI losses: e.g., <u>antiemetics</u> for <u>nausea and vomiting</u>, <u>antidiarrheal drugs</u>

* <u>Third space fluid loss</u>: e.g., treatment for <u>pancreatitis</u> or <u>bowel obstruction</u>

* Increased <u>insensible fluid losses</u>: e.g., treatment for <u>burns</u>, <u>antipyretic therapy</u> for <u>fever</u>

* Renal losses: e.g., cessation of <u>diuretics</u>, <u>treatment for diabetes</u> insipidus

* <u>Supportive care</u>: e.g., treating any concomitant <u>electrolyte</u> abnormalities (e.g., <u>hyponatremia</u>, <u>hypokalemia</u>)

* Next steps (once hemodynamically stable)

* Continue with <u>replacement of ongoing fluid loss</u> as needed.

* Attempt <u>oral rehydration therapy</u>.

---

## Cardiogenic shock

### Etiology




* <u>Myocardial infarction</u> (<u>MI</u>): most common cause

* <u>Arrhythmias</u>

* <u>Heart failure</u>

* <u>Cardiomyopathy</u>

* <u>Myocarditis</u>

* <u>Ventricular septal defect</u>, ventricular rupture

* Valve defects: severe aortic or <u>mitral regurgitation</u>

* <u>Blunt cardiac trauma</u>

* Certain drugs (e.g., <u>beta blockers</u>, <u>calcium channel blockers</u>)





### Pathophysiology




* Underlying event causes dysfunction of the <u>heart</u> → ↓ cardiac contractility and/or <u>SV</u> → ↓ CO

* <u>Systemic circulation</u>: ↓ CO and ↓ BP → ↑ <u>catecholamines</u> → <u>vasoconstriction</u> and ↑ <u>myocardial</u> oxygen demand → ↑ <u>renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system</u> → further ↑ <u>vasoconstriction</u> and retention of <u>sodium</u> and water → shunting of blood to the <u>brain</u> and vital organs → insufficient <u>perfusion</u> of peripheral organs

* <u>Pulmonary circulation</u>: ↓ cardiac contractility and/or ↓ <u>SV</u> → ↑ pulmonary <u>hydrostatic pressure</u> → <u>pulmonary edema</u>





### Management approach [[57]](/library/vSbAYt)




* Determine the type of <u>cardiogenic shock</u> according to the <u>classification of acute heart failure</u>. 

* No evidence of congestion (“dry and cold”)

* Evidence of congestion (“wet and cold”)

* Tailor initial treatment according to type.

* Provide <u>supportive care</u>.

* Elevate the patient's head.

* Provide <u>respiratory support for AHF</u> if there are <u>signs of fluid overload</u>.

* Stop or modify medication that can worsen the symptoms (e.g., <u>antihypertensives</u>).

* Treat the underlying cause (e.g., <u>revascularization</u> in <u>MI</u>).

* See also “<u>Management of acute heart failure</u>.”





| <br>Management of cardiogenic shock [[47]](/library/ipYJ6J)[[57]](/library/vSbAYt)[[58]](/library/Blbz_F)<br> |  |
| --- | --- |
| Classification | <br>Treatment (see “<u>Vasopressors and inotropes</u>” for dosages)<br> |
| Dry and cold | <br><br>* Fluid bolus only in cases of <u>hypotension</u> and/or <u>PCWP</u> < 15 mm Hg<br><br>* Consider a <u>fluid challenge</u> (250–500 mL). [[47]](/library/ipYJ6J)[[59]](/library/SpYyKJ)<br><br>* Assess <u>fluid responsiveness</u>; consider additional bolus if the patient is responsive to fluid.  [[60]](/library/IibYGt)<br><br>* Reassess for <u>clinical signs of volume overload</u>.<br><br>* If shock persists, start a <u>vasopressor</u>, ideally, <u>norepinephrine</u>.<br><br>* Administer <u>inotropic</u> support if <u>hypoperfusion</u> persists despite fluids and <u>vasopressors</u>.  [[46]](/library/2pYTKJ)<br><br>* <u>Dobutamine</u>  [[39]](/library/Nob-Xu)[[47]](/library/ipYJ6J)<br><br>* <u>Milrinone</u>  [[41]](/library/yLbdZu)<br><br>* <u>Dopamine</u><br><br><br> |
| Wet and cold | <br><br>* Administer <u>inotropic</u> therapy to maintain <u>perfusion</u>.<br><br>* If shock persists, start a <u>vasopressor</u> (ideally, <u>norepinephrine</u>).<br><br>* Once systolic BP is > 90 mm Hg, start <u>diuretic therapy for AHF</u>.<br><br>* If symptoms persist, start <u>treatment for refractory AHF</u>.<br><br><br> |





> [!WARNING]
> <u>IV fluids</u> can worsen <u>cardiogenic pulmonary edema</u> in most cases of <u>cardiogenic shock</u>. Check <u>fluid responsiveness</u> prior to administration of <u>fluid therapy</u>.




> [!WARNING]
> Avoid <u>inotropes</u> in patients with <u>left ventricular outflow tract obstruction</u> (e.g., <u>hypertrophic cardiomyopathy</u>, <u>aortic stenosis</u>). [[61]](/library/dlboDF)

---

## Obstructive shock

### Etiology




* ↓ <u>Diastolic</u> filling

* <u>Cardiac tamponade</u>

* <u>Constrictive pericarditis</u>

* <u>Restrictive cardiomyopathy</u>

* ↓ <u>Venous return</u>

* <u>Tension pneumothorax</u>

* Intrathoracic <u>tumor</u>

* <u>Abdominal compartment syndrome</u>

* ↑ Ventricular <u>afterload</u>

* <u>Massive pulmonary embolism</u> (<u>PE</u>)

* <u>Aortic dissection</u>

* <u>Aortic stenosis</u>

* Large systemic <u>emboli</u>

* Severe <u>pulmonary hypertension</u>





### Pathophysiology [[6]](/library/SlXywy)




* Common mechanism: obstruction of the <u>heart</u> or its great vessels → inability of the <u>heart</u> to circulate blood → ↓ CO → compensatory ↑ <u>SVR</u>

* <u>Pulmonary embolism</u> or severe <u>PAH</u>

* Obstructions of the pulmonary vasculature → ↓ <u>PCWP</u> → ↑ RV pressure → <u>right heart failure</u>

* ↑ RV pressure → ↑ pressure on LV by the RV → ↓ LV <u>diastolic</u> filling → ↓ CO

* <u>Right heart failure</u> → ↓ LV <u>preload</u> → ↓ CO

* <u>Tension pneumothorax</u>

* ↑ Intrathoracic pressure → ↓ <u>venous return</u> → ↓ <u>preload</u> → ↓ <u>PCWP</u>

* ↑ Intrathoracic pressure → ↓ LV <u>diastolic</u> filling → ↓ CO

* <u>Cardiac tamponade</u>

* ↑ <u>Pericardial</u> pressure → ↑ RV pressure → ↓ RV <u>diastolic</u> filling → <u>right heart failure</u>

* ↑ <u>Pericardial</u> pressure → ↑ LV pressure → ↓ LV <u>diastolic</u> filling → ↓ CO

* ↑ LV pressure → ↑ <u>PCWP</u> → ↑ RV pressure

* <u>Right heart failure</u> → ↓ LV <u>preload</u> → ↓ CO





> [!TIP]
> Despite manifesting with high <u>PCWP</u>, many causes of <u>obstructive shock</u> (e.g., severe <u>pulmonary hypertension</u>, <u>cardiac tamponade</u>) are considered <u>preload-dependent</u> states. [[6]](/library/SlXywy)




> [!NOTE]
> Elevation and equalization of pressures in all the cardiac chambers differentiate <u>cardiac tamponade</u> from other causes of <u>obstructive shock</u>.




### Treatment




* Provide <u>immediate hemodynamic support</u>.

* <u>Fluid resuscitation</u> for patients who are <u>preload-dependent</u> and/or <u>fluid responsive</u>

* Consider <u>vasopressors</u> or <u>inotropic</u> support.

* Treatment based on the underlying cause, including:

* <u>Pericardiocentesis</u> for <u>cardiac tamponade</u>

* <u>Thrombolytic therapy in PE</u> or <u>embolectomy in PE</u>

* <u>Needle thoracostomy</u> followed by <u>chest tube placement</u> or <u>surgery</u> for <u>tension pneumothorax</u>





![Management of pneumothorax](media/zjsoa0vo8yi1gvv78c5ngex4.jpg)

Management of pneumothorax

---

## Distributive shock

### Etiology




* <u>Septic shock</u> 

* Infection (especially <u>gram-negative bacteria</u>) and <u>bacteremia</u>

* See “Etiology” in “<u>Sepsis</u>.”

* <u>Anaphylactic shock</u>

* Drug reactions;  (e.g., <u>sulfa drugs</u>, contrast medium <u>allergy</u>)

* <u>Insect stings</u> or bites (e.g., <u>bee stings</u>)

* <u>Food allergies</u> (e.g., peanuts)

* <u>Neurogenic shock</u>

* <u>Spinal cord injury</u> (SCI)

* <u>Traumatic brain injury</u>

* Cerebral hemorrhage

* <u>Neuraxial anesthesia</u>

* <u>Acute adrenal insufficiency</u>

* <u>Stress</u> in patients with underlying <u>adrenal insufficiency</u>

* Sudden discontinuation of <u>glucocorticoids</u> after prolonged <u>glucocorticoid</u> therapy

* See “<u>Adrenal crisis</u>” for details.





### Pathophysiology




* Common mechanism: <u>vasodilation</u> with or without <u>capillary</u> leakage → redistribution of fluid from the <u>intravascular</u> to the extravascular compartment

* <u>Septic shock</u> 

* Specific mechanisms

* Dysregulated host response to infection → <u>capillary leakage</u> and systemic <u>vasodilation</u> → acute organ dysfunction

* Circulating inflammatory <u>cytokines</u> → <u>myocardial</u> <u>depression</u>

* Effect on <u>cardiac output</u>

* Early: compensatory ↑ HR and contractility → ↑ CO (<u>hyperdynamic state</u> or “warm shock”)

* Late: ↓ <u>preload</u> and direct <u>myocardial</u> <u>depression</u> by <u>cytokines</u> → ↓ CO (hypodynamic state or “cold shock”) [[62]](/library/-sXDxz)

* <u>Neurogenic shock</u>

* Specific mechanism: damage of autonomic pathways → loss of <u>sympathetic</u> vascular tone → unopposed <u>vagal</u> tone → peripheral <u>vasodilation</u> → pooling of peripheral blood

* Effect on <u>cardiac output</u>: can last days to weeks after <u>spinal cord injury</u> [[63]](/library/78X4L-)[[64]](/library/H8XKL-)

* Unopposed <u>vagal</u> effect → ↓ HR

* ↓ <u>Catecholamines</u> released from the <u>sympathetic</u> outflow → absent compensatory increases in HR and cardiac contractility

* <u>Anaphylactic shock</u>

* Specific mechanism: immunologic <u>anaphylaxis</u> (<u>type I hypersensitivity reaction</u>; <u>IgE</u>-mediated) or nonimmunologic <u>anaphylaxis</u> (not <u>IgE</u>-mediated) → <u>degranulation</u> of <u>mast cells</u> → massive <u>histamine</u> release → systemic <u>vasodilation</u> and increased <u>capillary leakage</u>

* Effect on <u>cardiac output</u>

* Early: compensatory ↑ HR and ↑ <u>SV</u> → ↑ CO

* Late: ↓ vascular tone and ↑ <u>capillary</u> permeability → ↓ <u>venous return</u> → ↓ CO → ↓ coronary <u>perfusion</u> → ↓ contractility → ↓↓ CO [[65]](/library/XGX9Bz)





### Key treatment components




* Volume expansion with <u>fluid resuscitation</u>

* Reversal of <u>vasodilation</u> with <u>vasopressors</u>

* Treatment of the underlying condition (e.g., <u>antibiotics</u>, removal of inciting <u>allergens</u>, spinal decompression <u>surgery</u>, <u>glucocorticoid</u> replacement)

---

## Septic shock

### Definition




* <u>Sepsis</u> and both of the following, despite adequate <u>fluid therapy</u> (i.e., <u>normovolemic</u> patients):

* <u>Vasopressors</u> required to maintain an <u>MAP</u> ≥ 65 mm Hg

* Serum <u>lactate</u> > 18 mg/dL

* See also “<u>Sepsis definitions</u>.”





### Management of septic shock




See “<u>Management of sepsis</u>” for details on evaluation and definitive <u>treatment of sepsis</u>. The following recommendations relate to <u>septic shock</u> and are consistent with the 2016 and 2018 Surviving <u>Sepsis</u> Campaign guidelines: [[12]](/library/1Ba2-5)[[36]](/library/APbRhF)




* Begin interventions of the <u>hour-1 bundle</u> for <u>sepsis</u>, including:

* <u>Fluid resuscitation</u>: rapid <u>crystalloid</u> infusion of 30 mL/kg [[12]](/library/1Ba2-5)[[36]](/library/APbRhF)

* <u>Antibiotic therapy for sepsis</u>

* Consider protocolized resuscitation target strategies in addition to standard <u>hemodynamic monitoring parameters</u>.

* The threshold for beginning <u>vasopressors for septic shock</u> should be low.

* Consider <u>corticosteroids</u> (e.g., <u>hydrocortisone</u>  DOSAGE) for shock refractory to the first <u>vasopressor</u>.





> [!TIP]
> 200–340 oz of <u>IV fluids</u> may be necessary during the first 24 hours. [[66]](/library/35YSPp)




![Septic shock: diagnosis & management](media/small_62b41db01d4d99.94127826.jpg)

Septic shock: diagnosis & management




#### Protocolized resuscitation target strategies  [[12]](/library/1Ba2-5)[[36]](/library/APbRhF)[[67]](/library/k4bmjF)




There is insufficient evidence to support the use of one target over the others in order to inform decisions about escalating <u>hemodynamic support</u>.  [[12]](/library/1Ba2-5)




* Lactate-guided fluid resuscitation strategy  [[36]](/library/APbRhF)[[67]](/library/k4bmjF)

* If the initial <u>lactate</u> level is elevated (> 2 mmol/L), remeasure every 2–4 hours until normalized.

* Treatment target: 20% decrease in serum <u>lactate</u> every 2–4 hours until normal

* Down-trending <u>lactate</u>: Continue <u>fluid resuscitation</u> until normalized.

* Persistent <u>hypotension</u> and/or <u>lactate</u> does not decrease as expected: aggressive <u>fluid resuscitation</u> and consider adding <u>vasopressors</u>.

* Disadvantages [[67]](/library/k4bmjF)[[68]](/library/skbt6F)

* Elevated <u>lactate</u> is not specific to <u>sepsis</u>.

* This strategy may lead to <u>fluid overload</u>.

* Early goal-directed therapy (<u>EGDT</u>)  [[12]](/library/1Ba2-5)
* Treatment targets

* <u>CVP</u> â¥ 8 cm HâO  [[12]](/library/1Ba2-5)

* <u>Central venous O<sub>2</sub>saturation</u> ≥ 70%

* <u>MAP</u> treatment target: ≥ 65 mm Hg





#### Vasopressors for septic shock [[12]](/library/1Ba2-5)[[36]](/library/APbRhF)[[67]](/library/k4bmjF)[[68]](/library/skbt6F)[[69]](/library/gmbFU8)




* Indications: persistent <u>hypotension</u> during or after <u>fluid resuscitation</u>

* Goal: maintain <u>MAP</u> ≥ 65 mm Hg [[12]](/library/1Ba2-5)

* Stepwise escalation (see “<u>Vasopressors and inotropes</u>” for dosages)

* First-line: <u>norepinephrine</u>

* If <u>MAP</u> is still low after <u>norepinephrine</u>:

* Add <u>vasopressin</u>

* OR add continuous IV <u>epinephrine infusion</u> (<u>off-label</u>)

* To decrease <u>norepinephrine</u> dosage: Add <u>vasopressin</u>.

* Additional options

* <u>Dopamine</u>

* Indicated as an alternative <u>vasopressor</u> in select cases (e.g., low risk of <u>tachyarrhythmia</u>, <u>bradycardia</u>) [[12]](/library/1Ba2-5)

* Should not be used for renal protection [[12]](/library/1Ba2-5)

* <u>Dobutamine</u>: Consider for <u>hypoperfusion</u> that persists despite fluids and initial <u>vasopressors</u>. [[12]](/library/1Ba2-5)

---

## Anaphylactic shock

### Initial management [[66]](/library/35YSPp)[[70]](/library/K1YU3L)[[71]](/library/QuYuII)




* Assess and <u>secure the airway</u> as needed (see “<u>Airway management and ventilation in anaphylaxis</u>”).

* Remove <u>allergen</u> when possible (e.g., stop medication or IV contrast).

* Administer <u>epinephrine</u> IM 1:1,000 as soon as possible and repeat as needed.

* Provide <u>immediate hemodynamic support</u> with <u>fluid resuscitation</u>.

* See also “<u>Management of anaphylaxis</u>” for further details.





> [!WARNING]
> Adjunctive treatment (<u>antihistamines</u> and <u>corticosteroids</u>) should only be administered after the initial resuscitation measures (<u>IM epinephrine</u>, fluids and/or <u>vasopressors</u>) have been given.




### Refractory <u>anaphylactic shock</u> [[66]](/library/35YSPp)[[70]](/library/K1YU3L)[[71]](/library/QuYuII)




* Refractory to repeated <u>IM epinephrine</u> and fluids: Start continuous IV <u>epinephrine infusion</u> 1:1,000,000 (1 mcg/mL).

* Refractory to IV <u>epinephrine infusion</u>

* Administer IV <u>glucagon</u> DOSAGE, especially if the patient is on a <u>beta blocker</u>.

* Consider combination with other <u>vasopressors</u>: e.g., <u>vasopressin</u>, <u>norepinephrine</u>, <u>dopamine</u>, and <u>phenylephrine</u>.

* Ensure adequate fluid status.

* Consider consulting <u>ECMO</u> team if all other measures fail.

---

## Neurogenic shock

### Diagnosis




<u>Neurogenic shock</u> is a <u>clinical diagnosis</u>.




* Classic presentation: <u>hypotension</u>, <u>bradycardia</u>, <u>vasodilation</u>  [[5]](/library/BNXzWA)

* Exclude other reasons for shock (e.g., other injuries).

* Other neurological deficits may be present.





> [!NOTE]
> In a patient who develops <u>low blood pressure</u> following high-energy trauma, <u>neurogenic shock</u> is a diagnosis of exclusion that is made after <u>hypovolemic</u> and <u>obstructive shock</u> have been ruled out.




### Management [[72]](/library/D1d1QK0)[[73]](/library/CIWqU50)[[74]](/library/YvXnA-)[[75]](/library/o1Y03L)




The following reviews the management of <u>neurogenic shock</u> from <u>spinal cord injury</u>, for <u>brain injury</u>-associated shock, see “<u>Blood pressure control in brain injury</u>.”




* Treatment

* <u>Fluid resuscitation</u>

* First-line therapy

* Avoid aggressive fluid boluses in patients with poor <u>fluid responsiveness</u>, because of the risk of <u>fluid overload</u>.

* <u>Vasopressors</u>: commonly required as shock is often refractory to fluids

* Lesions above T6: Consider <u>norepinephrine</u> or <u>dopamine</u>.  [[75]](/library/o1Y03L)

* Lesions below T6: Consider <u>phenylephrine</u>.  [[75]](/library/o1Y03L)

* Consider <u>atropine</u>  DOSAGE or cardiac pacing to treat <u>bradycardia</u> (see “<u>Unstable bradycardia</u>” for details). [[76]](/library/CNXqWA)

* Consult a <u>spine</u> <u>surgeon</u> early to evaluate whether the patient is a candidate for urgent spinal decompression.

* Monitoring

* <u>Insert a urinary catheter</u> early.  [[77]](/library/0vXeA-)

* <u>Hemodynamic targets</u> should be individualized in consultation with a specialist. 

* Avoid <u>hypotension</u> (systolic BP < 90 mm Hg).

* Consider maintaining a <u>MAP</u> of 75–90 mm Hg during the first 3–7 days after <u>spinal cord injury</u>.  [[72]](/library/D1d1QK0)[[73]](/library/CIWqU50)[[74]](/library/YvXnA-)

* Laboratory <u>perfusion parameters</u> (e.g., <u>lactate</u>, <u>base deficit</u>) are typically more reliable markers of <u>perfusion</u> than <u>MAP</u> in patients with SCI.

* Monitor for cardiovascular complications (e.g., <u>ACS</u>, <u>stroke</u>).

* <u>Supportive care</u> [[75]](/library/o1Y03L)

* Prevent <u>hypothermia</u> ; monitor temperature frequently and use warm <u>IV fluids</u> or warming devices as needed.

* Patients may have <u>allodynia</u>; careful patient handling and <u>pain management</u> are required.

* <u>Vasovagal</u> responses can be increased and can lead to <u>refractory shock</u>.

* <u>Autonomic dysreflexia</u>  and vascular dysfunction may be present and can complicate management and recovery. [[76]](/library/CNXqWA)[[78]](/library/9NXNWA)





> [!WARNING]
> Patients with <u>neurogenic shock</u> can have increased <u>vasovagal</u> responses to common procedures (e.g., suctioning, <u>endotracheal intubation</u>), which can trigger rapid changes in <u>heart rate</u> and blood pressure and increase the risk for complications and <u>refractory shock</u>. [[79]](/library/xNXEWA)

---

## Complications

* General

* Cardiovascular collapse

* <u>Acute renal failure</u> (due to prolonged tissue <u>hypoperfusion</u>)

* <u>Delirium</u>

* Specific shock subtypes

* <u>Airway obstruction</u> (<u>anaphylactic shock</u>)

* <u>Pulmonary edema</u> (<u>cardiogenic shock</u>)

* <u>Disseminated intravascular coagulation</u> (<u>hemorrhagic shock</u> and <u>septic shock</u>)

* <u>Iatrogenic</u>

* <u>Nosocomial infections</u>: e.g., <u>CLABSI</u>, <u>VAP</u>

* <u>Complications of mechanical ventilation</u>

* <u>Complications of IV fluid therapy</u>




We list the most important complications. The selection is not exhaustive.

---

## Refractory shock

Rescue therapies for shock are for patients who remain in shock despite adequate treatment of the underlying cause. These treatments should be given in consultation with a specialist, and they include: [[3]](/library/Tob6Yu)




* <u>Corticosteroids</u> (e.g., <u>hydrocortisone</u>): for suspected critical illness-related corticosteroid insufficiency (<u>CIRCI</u>)  [[38]](/library/JVXsvC)[[80]](/library/smXtSA)

* Diagnosis of <u>CIRCI</u> is based on the presence of critical illness plus one of the following :

* Increase in <u>cortisol</u> level of < 9 mcg/dL after an <u>ACTH stimulation test</u>

* Random plasma <u>cortisol</u> 10–15 mcg/dL  [[38]](/library/JVXsvC)[[80]](/library/smXtSA)

* Positive hemodynamic response (e.g., reduced need for <u>vasopressors</u>) to <u>hydrocortisone</u> 50–300 mg IV

* See also “<u>Adrenal crisis</u>.”

* <u>Bicarbonate</u> (e.g., <u>8.4% sodium bicarbonate</u> DOSAGE) [[3]](/library/Tob6Yu)

* For correction of severe <u>metabolic acidosis</u> (e.g., <u>pH</u> < 7.1)

* Tailor treatment to the patient's <u>bicarbonate</u> deficit and monitor HCO<sub>3</sub> levels and <u>pH</u> frequently (e.g., initially every 2 hours).  [[81]](/library/BSXzbB)

* <u>Mechanical circulatory support</u>

* Consider <u>ECMO</u> for <u>severe ARDS</u>, refractory <u>respiratory failure</u>, or refractory <u>heart failure</u>.

* Consider <u>IABP</u> and <u>LVAD</u> for refractory <u>cardiogenic shock</u>.
